prompt: What does a context in `~/.kube/config` name?
hint: Three things, one of them optional.

choices.text: One cluster and nothing else
choices.why: A context also names the credentials, and can carry a namespace.

choices.text: A cluster, a user, and optionally a namespace
choices.why: Right. Switching context switches all three at once.

choices.text: A namespace inside the cluster you are working on
choices.why: A namespace can be part of a context, but the context also says which cluster and as whom.

choices.text: A set of objects kubectl has applied before
choices.why: The file keeps no record of objects; that lives in the cluster.

prompt: A deploy script runs against production every night. Why is `kubectl --context prod apply -f …` safer in it than `kubectl config use-context prod` followed by `kubectl apply -f …`?

choices.text: `--context` encrypts the connection and `use-context` does not
choices.why: Both reach the same API server over the same TLS connection.

choices.text: `use-context` needs administrator rights on the cluster
choices.why: It only edits a local file; the cluster never hears about it.

choices.text: `use-context` stays in the file for every later command
choices.why: Right. The next command anyone types on that machine goes to production too; `--context` affects one command.

choices.text: `--context` refuses to run if the cluster is unreachable
choices.why: Both fail the same way when the cluster cannot be reached.

prompt: After `kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=dev`, a colleague says the `dev` namespace is now isolated from `default`. What does this lesson say?
hint: What does a namespace change, by itself?

choices.text: Right: pods in `dev` can no longer reach `default`
choices.why: Nothing about the network changed; only where names are looked up.

choices.text: Only the lookup changed; isolation needs more
choices.why: Right. A namespace changes where a name is looked up; lessons 20 and 24 add limits and network rules.

choices.text: The command also limited how much CPU `dev` may use
choices.why: Limits per namespace are quotas, a separate object (lesson 20).

choices.text: It moved the pods of `default` into `dev`
choices.why: It edited the kubeconfig file; no object in the cluster moved.

prompt: Ana ran `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml` twice without editing the file. What did the second run print?

choices.text: An error, because `web` already existed
choices.why: That is what `kubectl create` does; `apply` compares and acts on the difference.

choices.text: `created`, and a second deployment appeared
choices.why: Names are unique in a namespace; the same file names the same object.

choices.text: `deployment.apps/web unchanged`
choices.why: Right. Nothing differed, so nothing was sent; that is what makes apply safe to repeat.

choices.text: `configured`, because apply always rewrites the object
choices.why: It printed `configured` only after the file changed.

prompt: After `kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5`, `kubectl diff -f deployment.yaml` printed `-  replicas: 5` and `+  replicas: 3`. What does that diff describe?
hint: The minus side is the live object.

choices.text: What applying the file would change in the live object
choices.why: Right. The cluster has drifted to 5, and the file would take it back to 3.

choices.text: What changed in the file since its last commit to the repository
choices.why: kubectl diff compares the file with the cluster, not with git.

choices.text: A conflict apply cannot resolve
choices.why: apply resolved it: the next listing showed 3/3.

choices.text: Two replicas that failed to start
choices.why: The numbers are the spec on each side; nothing about failures is in it.

prompt: To see what `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml` would change, without changing anything, run `kubectl ___ -f deployment.yaml`.
hint: Its output is a unified diff.

prompt: Why does kubectl store the `last-applied-configuration` annotation on the object?
hint: A field missing from the file can mean two different things.

choices.text: To let the cluster roll back to it after a failure
choices.why: Rollbacks use ReplicaSets and history (lesson 35), not this annotation.

choices.text: To tell a field you removed from one somebody else set
choices.why: Right. Without the last file, apply could not know whether to delete a field that is absent.

choices.text: Because the API server refuses objects without it
choices.why: `kubectl create` makes objects without it; it is kubectl's bookkeeping.

choices.text: To record who applied the file and when
choices.why: It holds the file's content, not an author or a time.

prompt: Match each command with what it does.
hint: Two of them never change the cluster.

pairs.right: Makes the cluster match the file
Prints an object without sending it
Removes the objects the file names

right_distractors: Copies the cluster's objects into the file

prompt: During an incident Ana scaled to 5 by hand, and it helped. The next morning a pipeline ran `kubectl apply -f` from git. What happened, and what should she have done?
hint: The file in git still said 3.

choices.text: Nothing; apply keeps changes made by hand
choices.why: apply makes the cluster match the file, so it took it back to 3.

choices.text: apply failed on the conflict; she had to delete the deployment
choices.why: There was no failure; the drift was simply undone.

choices.text: It went back to 3; the change should also have gone into the file
choices.why: Right. A fix that should still be true tomorrow belongs in git, or the next apply undoes it.

choices.text: It went to 8, adding the file's 3 to the 5 by hand
choices.why: Fields are replaced, never added together.
